verse.text: Paul, a slave of Christ Jesus, called to be an apostle, set apart for the good news of God,
verse.note: The Greek word is the ordinary term for a slave, a person owned by a master, and Paul applies it to himself in relation to Christ. Most English versions soften it to “servant,” and some scholars also hear an echo of the Old Testament’s honorific “servant of the Lord.” The plain sense of ownership and total allegiance is kept here.

Traditionally “gospel,” which is now a religious term or the name of a book. The Greek was an ordinary word for a public announcement of good news, used also of imperial proclamations. Many modern translations alternate between “gospel” and “good news.”

verse.text: which he promised beforehand through his prophets in the holy Scriptures,
concerning his Son, who was born a descendant of David according to the flesh,
who was appointed Son of God in power according to the Spirit of holiness by resurrection from the dead—Jesus Christ our Lord,
verse.note: Many English versions have “declared,” which suggests that the resurrection only made known what Jesus already was. In the usage of the period the verb means to appoint, designate or fix, and most lexicons and recent commentators render it that way here. “In power” may go with “Son of God” (installed as Son of God in power, a new stage for one already called God’s Son in verse 3) or with “appointed” (powerfully appointed).

The phrase occurs only here in the New Testament and reflects a Hebrew way of saying “Holy Spirit.” Most interpreters take it as God’s Spirit, and it is capitalized accordingly. A minority take it as Jesus’s own holy spirit or divine nature, set against “according to the flesh” in verse 3.

verse.text: through whom we received grace and apostleship to bring about the obedience of faith among all the Gentiles for the sake of his name,
verse.note: The Greek is as compact as the English and can mean the obedience that consists in faith, the obedience that springs from faith, or both at once. The literal phrase is kept so as not to decide the question. The same phrase returns at the close of the letter (16:26).

The Greek word means “nations” or “peoples,” and in the plural it is the regular Jewish term for the non-Jewish peoples; English uses “Gentiles” and “nations” for the one Greek word. “Among all the nations” is possible here, but Paul’s commission was specifically to non-Jews, and verse 13 uses the same word in that sense.

verse.text: among whom you also are called to belong to Jesus Christ—
to all in Rome who are loved by God, called to be holy ones: Grace to you and peace from God our Father and the Lord Jesus Christ.
verse.note: Traditionally “saints,” which now suggests canonized individuals or people of exceptional virtue. Paul uses the word for all believers as people set apart for God, echoing the Septuagint’s language for Israel. Other translations keep “saints” or use “God’s holy people.”

verse.text: First, I thank my God through Jesus Christ for all of you, because your faith is being proclaimed in the whole world.
For God, whom I serve in my spirit in the good news of his Son, is my witness how unceasingly I make mention of you
always in my prayers, asking that somehow, now at last, I may succeed by God’s will in coming to you.
For I long to see you, so that I may share with you some spiritual gift to strengthen you—
that is, that we may be encouraged together while I am among you, through one another’s faith, both yours and mine.

I do not want you to be unaware, brothers and sisters, that I have often planned to come to you—and have been prevented until now—so that I might have some fruit among you too, just as among the rest of the Gentiles.
verse.note: Traditionally “brethren” or “brothers.” The Greek masculine plural was the normal way to address a mixed group of men and women, and Paul is writing to the whole community in Rome. Many recent translations render it this way.

verse.text: I am a debtor both to Greeks and to barbarians, both to the wise and to the foolish;
verse.note: To Greek speakers a “barbarian” was anyone who did not speak Greek or share Greek culture; the word carried cultural condescension but did not mean “savage.” “Greeks and barbarians” was a stock way of saying all humankind from the Greek point of view.

verse.text: so, for my part, I am eager to proclaim the good news to you also who are in Rome.
For I am not ashamed of the good news, for it is the power of God for salvation to everyone who believes, to the Jew first and also to the Greek.
For in it the righteousness of God is revealed from faith to faith, as it is written: “The righteous will live by faith.”
verse.note: Greek has a single word-family where English has two: “righteous” and “just,” “righteousness” and “justice,” “justify.” The phrase may mean God’s own righteousness, especially his action to set things right, or a right standing that comes from God; interpreters are divided. “Righteousness” is kept because “the justice of God” would suggest punishing justice to a modern reader, though some scholars prefer “justice” or “covenant faithfulness.”

The phrase is compressed and disputed. It may be an idiom of emphasis (“by faith from first to last”), or mean that the revelation starts from faith and leads to faith, or, as some argue, that it moves from God’s or Christ’s faithfulness to human faith. The literal wording leaves these options open.

note.term: The righteous will live by faith
note.traditional: The just shall live by faith

verse.note: A quotation of Habakkuk 2:4. “By faith” can be attached to “will live,” as here, or to “the righteous” (“the one who is righteous by faith will live”); both readings have strong scholarly support. The Greek phrase behind “by faith” is the same one rendered “from faith” earlier in the verse, and the noun can also mean “faithfulness.”

verse.text: For the wrath of God is revealed from heaven against all the ungodliness and unrighteousness of people who suppress the truth by their unrighteousness,
because what can be known about God is plain among them, for God has made it plain to them.
For since the creation of the world, what is unseen of him—his eternal power and divine nature—has been clearly seen, being understood through the things he has made, so that they are without excuse,
because, though they knew God, they did not glorify him as God or give him thanks; instead they became futile in their reasoning, and their senseless hearts were darkened.
Claiming to be wise, they became fools,
and exchanged the glory of the immortal God for the likeness of an image of a mortal human being, and of birds and four-footed animals and creeping things.
Therefore God handed them over, in the desires of their hearts, to impurity, to the dishonoring of their bodies among themselves,

note.traditional: gave them up; gave them over

verse.note: Traditionally “gave them up” or “gave them over.” The verb is the ordinary word for transferring someone into another’s custody or power, the same word used in the Gospels for Jesus being handed over to the authorities. It recurs as a refrain in verses 24, 26 and 28: God’s judgment takes the form of leaving people in the grip of what they have chosen.

verse.text: since they exchanged the truth of God for the lie, and revered and served the creation rather than the Creator, who is blessed forever. Amen.
For this reason God handed them over to dishonorable passions. For their females exchanged natural relations for those contrary to nature,
verse.note: Most versions have “women” and “men” in verses 26–27. Paul does not use the ordinary words for women and men but the terms “female” and “male,” which many interpreters hear as an echo of the creation account (“male and female he created them,” Genesis 1:27). The rendering keeps that choice of words visible.

verse.text: and likewise the males too, leaving natural relations with the female, burned in their craving for one another, males with males committing shameful acts and receiving in themselves the due penalty for their error.
And just as they did not see fit to acknowledge God, God handed them over to an unfit mind, to do what ought not to be done.

note.traditional: reprobate mind; debased mind; depraved mind

verse.note: Traditionally “reprobate,” “debased” or “depraved” mind. The adjective means failing the test, rejected as unfit, and Paul plays on the related verb just before it: they did not “see fit” to acknowledge God, so God handed them over to a mind that is itself “unfit.” The rendering is chosen to keep that wordplay.

verse.text: They have been filled with every kind of unrighteousness, wickedness, greed, and malice. They are full of envy, murder, strife, deceit, and spite. They are gossips,
slanderers, God-haters, insolent, arrogant, boastful, inventors of evil, disobedient to parents,
verse.note: In earlier Greek this rare word normally meant “hated by a god,” and some interpreters take it that way here. Because the other items in the list are vices the people themselves practice, most translations and commentators take it in the active sense, “haters of God.”

verse.text: senseless, faithless, heartless, merciless.
Though they know God’s righteous decree, that those who practice such things deserve death, they not only do them but also approve of those who practice them.
verse.note: This translation normally renders the word “righteous requirement” or “righteous act.” Here its content is not something God requires people to do but his verdict that those who do such things deserve death, so “decree” is used, as in several major versions. The word belongs to the same family as “righteousness” in verse 17.

verse.text: Therefore you are without excuse, whoever you are, you who judge. For in judging the other person you condemn yourself, because you who judge practice the very same things.
verse.note: The Greek is a brusque vocative, literally “O person,” common in the lively question-and-answer style of ancient moral teachers, where the speaker argues with an imagined individual. “O man” is the traditional rendering, but it is archaic and sounds gender-specific where the Greek is not. The singular “you” throughout this chapter addresses that imagined partner, not a named individual; who he represents in verses 1–16 (a moralizing Gentile, a Jew, or anyone who judges) is debated.

verse.text: Now we know that God’s judgment on those who practice such things accords with truth.
And do you suppose, whoever you are, you who judge those who practice such things and yet do them yourself, that you will escape the judgment of God?
Or do you despise the riches of his kindness and forbearance and patience, not realizing that God’s kindness is leading you toward turning back?
verse.note: Most translations keep “repentance,” understood as including a change of life. In modern English, however, “repent” centers on feeling sorry, whereas the Greek word in Jewish usage carries the prophets’ call to return to God: a change of direction in mind and conduct. The related adjective in verse 5 is rendered “that refuses to turn back” (traditionally “impenitent” or “unrepentant”).

verse.text: But because of your hardness and your heart that refuses to turn back, you are storing up wrath for yourself on the day of wrath and of the revelation of the just judgment of God,
who will repay each person according to their works:

note.term: who will repay each person according to their works

verse.note: Paul’s wording closely follows the Greek version of Psalm 62:12 and Proverbs 24:12, though he does not mark it as a quotation. His first readers who knew the Scriptures would have recognized a settled principle of Jewish belief about God’s judgment.

verse.text: to those who by perseverance in good work seek glory and honor and immortality, eternal life;
but for those who act out of selfish ambition and disobey the truth but obey unrighteousness, wrath and fury.
verse.note: The word is rare before the New Testament; its earlier use, in Aristotle, concerns the self-interested pursuit of political office. Older versions linked it with a similar-sounding word for “strife” and translated “contentious,” but most scholars now prefer “selfish ambition” or “self-seeking.” The exact nuance remains uncertain.

verse.text: There will be affliction and distress for every human being who does what is evil, the Jew first and also the Greek,
but glory and honor and peace for everyone who does what is good, the Jew first and also the Greek.
For there is no partiality with God.
For all who have sinned without the law will also perish without the law, and all who have sinned under the law will be judged by the law.
For it is not the hearers of the law who are righteous in God’s sight; it is the doers of the law who will be justified.
verse.note: “Righteous” and “justified” here, “just judgment” in verse 5, “unrighteousness” in verse 8 and “righteous requirements” in verse 26 all belong to one Greek word-family, where English has two (righteous/just, righteousness/justice, justify). To be “justified” is to be declared in the right. How this statement that doers of the law will be justified fits with Paul’s later argument (3:20) is much discussed; some take it as hypothetical, others as a real description of the final judgment.

verse.text: For whenever Gentiles, who do not have the law, do by nature what the law requires, these, though they do not have the law, are a law to themselves.
verse.note: The Greek word means “nations” or “peoples”; in the plural, in Jewish usage, it regularly means the non-Jewish peoples. The same word is translated “nations” elsewhere when peoples as ethnic or political units are in view.

The phrase can be attached to what follows (Gentiles “do by nature what the law requires”) or to what precedes (Gentiles “who do not have the law by nature,” that is, by birth). Most translations take the first option, as here. A number of scholars prefer the second, noting the similar expression “uncircumcised by nature” in verse 27, and some of them think Paul has Gentile Christians in view.

verse.text: They show that the work of the law is written in their hearts, while their conscience also bears witness and their thoughts among themselves accuse or even excuse them
on the day when God judges what is hidden in people, according to my good news, through Christ Jesus.

note.term: on the day when God judges
note.traditional: in the day when God shall judge

verse.note: The link with verse 15 is abrupt, and some interpreters treat verses 14–15 as a parenthesis so that this verse continues verse 13 (“will be justified … on the day”). The verb can be read as present (“judges”) or future (“will judge”); the two differ only by an accent, which the earliest manuscripts did not write. Either way the final judgment is meant.

“Gospel” is the traditional rendering and many modern translations alternate between the two. The Greek was an ordinary word for a public announcement of good news, used also of imperial proclamations, whereas “gospel” now sounds like a purely religious term or a book title.

verse.text: But if you call yourself a Jew and rely on the law and boast in God
and know his will and discern what matters most, being instructed from the law,
and are confident that you yourself are a guide for the blind, a light for those in darkness,
an instructor of the foolish, a teacher of little children, having in the law the embodiment of knowledge and truth—
you, then, who teach another, do you not teach yourself? You who proclaim that one must not steal, do you steal?
You who say that one must not commit adultery, do you commit adultery? You who detest idols, do you rob temples?

note.traditional: dost thou commit sacrilege; do you rob temples

verse.note: The verb literally means to plunder a temple, and it also had a wider sense of committing sacrilege. Paul may mean actual theft or profit from goods taken from pagan shrines, which the Law forbade (Deuteronomy 7:25), or more loosely any irreverent treatment of what is sacred, perhaps even withholding what was owed to the Jerusalem temple. The precise reference is uncertain.

verse.text: You who boast in the law, do you dishonor God by transgressing the law?
For, just as it is written, “The name of God is blasphemed among the Gentiles because of you.”

note.term: “The name of God is blasphemed among the Gentiles because of you.”

verse.note: The quotation is from Isaiah 52:5 in the Greek version, which includes “because of you” and “among the Gentiles”; the Hebrew text is shorter. In Greek, “just as it is written” stands at the end of the sentence, an unusual position; it is moved forward here for English.

verse.text: For circumcision is of benefit if you practice the law; but if you are a transgressor of the law, your circumcision has become uncircumcision.
So if an uncircumcised man keeps the righteous requirements of the law, will not his uncircumcision be counted as circumcision?
And the one who is uncircumcised by nature yet fulfills the law will judge you, who have the letter and circumcision and yet are a transgressor of the law.
For a person is not a Jew by what is visible, nor is circumcision what is visible in the flesh.
Rather, a person is a Jew by what is hidden, and circumcision is of the heart, by the Spirit, not the letter. Such a person’s praise comes not from people but from God.

note.term: by the Spirit, not the letter
note.traditional: in the spirit, and not in the letter

verse.note: The Greek can mean “in spirit,” an inward as opposed to a literal circumcision, or “by the Spirit,” God’s Spirit as the one who brings it about. Many scholars favor the second in light of Paul’s similar contrast of Spirit and letter in Romans 7:6 and 2 Corinthians 3:6, but the first is also widely held. “Letter” means what is written, here the law as a written code.

Many interpreters hear a wordplay here: “Jew” derives from “Judah,” a name that Genesis 29:35 and 49:8 connect with the Hebrew verb “to praise.” The pun works in Hebrew and not in Greek, so it is uncertain whether Paul intended it or expected readers in Rome to catch it.

verse.text: What advantage, then, does the Jew have, or what is the benefit of circumcision?
Much in every way. First of all, they were entrusted with the oracles of God.
What if some were unfaithful? Will their unfaithfulness nullify the faithfulness of God?
verse.note: The Greek verb can mean either “were unfaithful” or “did not believe,” and older versions have the latter. Paul plays on one word-family across verses 2–3: “entrusted,” “unfaithful,” “unfaithfulness” and God’s “faithfulness” all share the root usually rendered “faith.” The contrast with God’s reliability favors “unfaithful,” and most modern translations agree.

verse.text: By no means! Let God be true though every person be a liar, as it is written: “So that you may be vindicated in your words and prevail when you are judged.”
verse.note: Paul quotes Psalm 51:4 in its Greek form (Psalm 50:6 in the Septuagint). The Greek verb form can be passive (“when you are judged”) or middle (“when you go to court”); the Hebrew has “when you judge.” The passive fits Paul’s picture of God being put on trial and winning his case, but the other reading is possible.

verse.text: But if our unrighteousness brings out the righteousness of God, what shall we say? Is God unjust when he inflicts his wrath? I am speaking in a human way.
verse.note: Greek has a single word-family where English has two: righteous and just, righteousness and justice, justify. “Vindicated” (verse 4), “unjust” here, “righteous” (verse 10), “justified” (verse 20) and “just” (verse 26) all belong to it. “Righteousness” is kept because “the justice of God” suggests punishing justice to a modern reader, where Paul chiefly means God’s action to put things right. Some scholars prefer “justice” or “covenant faithfulness.”

verse.text: By no means! For then how will God judge the world?
But if through my lie God’s truth has abounded to his glory, why am I also still judged as a sinner?
And why not say—as we are slandered, and as some claim that we say—“Let us do evil so that good may come”? Their condemnation is deserved.
What then? Are we any better off? Not at all, for we have already charged that Jews and Greeks alike are all under sin,
verse.note: The single Greek verb is rare in this form and its meaning is disputed. Most translations take it as “Do we (Jews) have an advantage?” It could also be passive, “Are we at a disadvantage?”, or mean “Are we making excuses?” The reply may likewise be “Not at all” or “Not altogether.”

verse.text: as it is written: “There is no one righteous, not even one;

note.term: There is no one righteous, not even one

verse.note: Verses 10–18 are a chain of Scripture quotations, mostly in the wording of the Greek Old Testament: Psalm 14:1–3, Psalm 5:9, Psalm 140:3, Psalm 10:7, Isaiah 59:7–8 and Psalm 36:1. Stringing texts together in this way was a recognized Jewish method of argument. Because these come from the Psalms and Isaiah, “the Law” in verse 19 evidently means the Scriptures as a whole.

text.q: there is no one who understands, there is no one who seeks God.
All have turned aside; together they have become worthless. There is no one who does good, there is not even one.
Their throat is an open grave; with their tongues they practice deceit; the venom of asps is under their lips.
Their mouth is full of cursing and bitterness.
Their feet are swift to shed blood;
ruin and misery are in their paths,
and the way of peace they have not known.
There is no fear of God before their eyes.”

verse.text: Now we know that whatever the Law says, it speaks to those within the Law, so that every mouth may be shut and the whole world be held accountable to God.
For by works of the law no flesh will be justified before him, since through the law comes knowledge of sin.
verse.note: The phrase means deeds done in obedience to the Law of Moses. Its focus is disputed: the traditional reading takes it as any effort to gain standing with God by keeping the commandments, while others think Paul has chiefly in view the practices that marked Jews off from Gentiles, such as circumcision, food laws and Sabbath. The verse echoes Psalm 143:2.

verse.text: But now, apart from law, the righteousness of God has been disclosed, attested by the Law and the Prophets—
the righteousness of God through faith in Jesus Christ for all who believe. For there is no distinction,
verse.note: The Greek is literally “faith of Jesus Christ,” and the grammar allows two readings: “faith in Jesus Christ” (trust placed in him) or “the faithfulness of Jesus Christ” (his own faithful obedience, through which God’s righteousness comes). The first is the traditional and still majority reading and is followed here; the second has substantial scholarly support.

verse.text: since all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God,
and are justified freely by his grace through the redemption that is in Christ Jesus.
God put him forward as a place of atonement, through faith, by his blood, to demonstrate his righteousness, because of the passing over of sins committed beforehand
verse.note: In the Greek Old Testament this word is the name of the gold cover of the ark, where blood was sprinkled on the Day of Atonement (Leviticus 16); Hebrews 9:5 uses it that way. The rendering lets that allusion be heard: Jesus is where atonement is made. Whether Paul means the ark’s cover, “propitiation” (turning away wrath) or “expiation” (removing sin) is a long-running dispute.

Older versions join the phrases: “through faith in his blood.” Most modern interpreters take them separately, both describing the atonement: it is received through faith and accomplished by his blood, that is, his death. Some read “through faithfulness,” referring to Christ’s or God’s own faithfulness.

verse.text: in the forbearance of God; it was to demonstrate his righteousness at the present time, so that he himself would be just and would justify the one who has faith in Jesus.
verse.note: Literally “the one who is of the faith of Jesus.” As in verse 22, the phrase can also be read as “the one who lives from the faithfulness of Jesus,” a reading with substantial scholarly support. The majority reading is followed here.

verse.text: Where, then, is boasting? It is shut out. By what kind of law? A law of works? No, but by a law of faith.
verse.note: The word is the one rendered “law” throughout the chapter. Many interpreters think Paul is playing on it here in the looser sense of “principle” or “rule,” and some translations render it so; others think he still means the Law of Moses, viewed either as demanding works or as calling for faith. “Law” is kept so that the reader can see the play on the word.

verse.text: For we hold that a person is justified by faith apart from works of the law.
Or is God the God of Jews only? Is he not the God of Gentiles also? Yes, of Gentiles also,
verse.note: The Greek word means “nations” or “peoples”; in the plural it was the usual Jewish term for all the non-Jewish peoples. This translation renders the one word as “Gentiles” or “nations” according to the sense.

verse.text: since God is one, and he will justify the circumcised by faith and the uncircumcised through that same faith.
Do we then nullify the law through faith? By no means! Rather, we uphold the law.
What then shall we say that Abraham, our forefather according to the flesh, found?

note.traditional: What then shall we say that Abraham, our forefather according to the flesh, has found?

verse.note: The Greek can also be punctuated as two questions: “What then shall we say? Have we found Abraham to be our forefather according to the flesh?” On that reading Paul is asking whether physical descent is what makes Abraham “our” father. Most translations take it as here. Manuscripts also differ on where the word “found” stands, and a few omit it.

verse.text: For if Abraham was justified by works, he has something to boast about, but not before God.
verse.note: Greek has a single word-family where English has two: “justify,” “just” and “justice” on one side, “righteous” and “righteousness” on the other. “Justified” here and “righteousness” in verse 3 are therefore the same root, and to be justified is to be declared or set in the right. Some scholars prefer “justice” or “covenant faithfulness” for the noun.

verse.text: For what does the Scripture say? “Abraham believed God, and it was counted to him as righteousness.”
verse.note: The verb is a bookkeeping term for entering something to a person’s account, and Paul uses it eleven times in this chapter. It is rendered “count” throughout so that the repetition is visible, including in verse 4 (wages) and verse 8 (sin). Other versions use “credited,” “reckoned” or “imputed.”

verse.text: Now to the one who works, the wages are not counted as a matter of grace but as a matter of debt.
verse.note: Most modern versions have “as a gift” or “as a favor” here. The Greek phrase is identical to the one in verse 16, and the word is Paul’s usual term for grace, so both verses are rendered alike to keep the link: wages are owed, but what God gives rests on grace.

verse.text: But to the one who does not work, but believes in the one who justifies the ungodly, his faith is counted as righteousness,
just as David also pronounces the blessing on the person to whom God counts righteousness apart from works:

text.q: “Blessed are those whose lawless deeds have been forgiven and whose sins have been covered;
blessed is the man against whom the Lord will never count sin.”

verse.text: Is this blessing, then, on the circumcised, or also on the uncircumcised? For we say that faith was counted to Abraham as righteousness.
How then was it counted? When he was circumcised or uncircumcised? Not when he was circumcised, but when he was uncircumcised.

And he received the sign of circumcision, a seal of the righteousness of the faith he had while uncircumcised, so that he would be the father of all who believe while uncircumcised, so that righteousness would be counted to them,
and the father of the circumcised, for those who are not merely circumcised but also follow in the footsteps of the faith that our father Abraham had while uncircumcised.

note.term: those who are not merely circumcised but also follow in the footsteps

verse.note: The Greek repeats the article in a way that, read strictly, would name two groups: the circumcised, and those who follow Abraham’s faith. Most interpreters judge the extra article a slip or a loose construction and understand one group, Jews who also share Abraham’s faith, as translated here.

verse.text: For the promise to Abraham or to his offspring, that he would be heir of the world, did not come through the law but through the righteousness of faith.
For if those who are of the law are heirs, faith has been emptied and the promise has been nullified.
For the law produces wrath; but where there is no law, there is no transgression either.

For this reason it is by faith, so that it may be a matter of grace, in order that the promise may be secure for all the offspring, not only for those who are of the law but also for those who are of the faith of Abraham. He is the father of us all,

as it is written, “I have made you the father of many nations.” He is our father in the presence of the God whom he believed, the one who gives life to the dead and calls the things that are not as though they were.
verse.note: The Greek word here is the same one translated “Gentiles” elsewhere in Romans (for example 3:29). In the quotation from Genesis 17:5 it means peoples in general, but Paul’s readers would have heard in it that Abraham is the father of Gentile believers as well as Jewish ones.

note.term: calls the things that are not as though they were
note.traditional: calls into existence the things that do not exist

verse.note: The Greek is literally “calling the things not being as being.” Many translations take this as God’s creative call that brings things into existence. The rendering here follows the more direct sense of the grammar: God speaks of what does not yet exist, such as Abraham’s many descendants, as already real. Both readings have strong scholarly support.

verse.text: Against hope, in hope he believed, and so became the father of many nations, according to what had been said: “So shall your offspring be.”
verse.note: The Greek construction can express result (“and so he became”), purpose (“in order to become”) or the content of what Abraham believed (“believed that he would become”). The result reading is adopted here; the others are grammatically possible, and translations are divided.

verse.text: And without weakening in faith, he considered his own body, as good as dead since he was about a hundred years old, and the deadness of Sarah’s womb,
verse.note: Many later manuscripts read “he did not consider his own body,” which the King James Version follows; the earliest witnesses lack the negative. With the negative, Abraham’s faith ignored the obstacles; without it, he faced them squarely and still believed. Some manuscripts also add “already” before “as good as dead.”

verse.text: yet with regard to the promise of God he did not waver in unbelief but was strengthened in faith, giving glory to God
and being fully convinced that what God had promised, he was also able to do.
That is why “it was counted to him as righteousness.”
Now the words “it was counted to him” were not written for his sake alone,
but also for our sake. It is going to be counted to us who believe in the one who raised Jesus our Lord from the dead,
who was handed over for our offenses and raised for our justification.
verse.note: The traditional “delivered” or “delivered up” is now unclear English. The verb is the ordinary word for handing someone into another’s power, and the Gospels use it for each stage of Jesus’ arrest and execution. The passive leaves the agent unstated, and the wording probably echoes Isaiah 53 in the Greek Old Testament.

The word means a wrongful act against God or another person. “Trespass,” the rendering of the Tyndale and King James tradition and of several modern versions, now mainly suggests entering property without permission. “Offense” is a standard gloss for the word, and its meaning is not disputed.

The same Greek preposition stands in both halves of the verse and normally means “because of.” The first half is naturally “because of our offenses.” The second is debated: either “because we had been justified” or, as most hold, “with a view to our justification.” “For” is used twice to keep the parallel and leave the question open.

verse.text: Therefore, having been justified by faith, we have peace with God through our Lord Jesus Christ,
verse.note: Greek has a single word-family where English has two: “justify,” “justification,” “righteous” and “righteousness” in this chapter all translate forms of the same root. To be “justified” is to be declared or set in the right. Translations into Latin and most other languages use their one word for “justice” throughout, and some scholars prefer “justice” or “covenant faithfulness” in English.

Many early and important manuscripts read “let us have peace” (a difference of one vowel, which was pronounced alike in the period). The edition translated here, with most translations, reads “we have peace,” mainly because Paul’s argument at this point is stating facts, not giving exhortations. The question remains disputed.

verse.text: through whom we have also obtained access by faith into this grace in which we stand, and we boast in the hope of the glory of God.
And not only that, but we also boast in our afflictions, knowing that affliction produces endurance,
verse.note: The traditional “tribulation” is now often heard as the name of a specific end-time period. In the period the word was an ordinary term for hardship or oppression pressing on a person. Modern versions vary here between “sufferings,” “afflictions” and “troubles.”

verse.text: and endurance produces proven character, and proven character produces hope.
And hope does not put us to shame, because God’s love has been poured out in our hearts through the Holy Spirit who was given to us.
verse.note: The Greek phrase “the love of God” can mean God’s love for us or our love for God. Verse 8, which speaks of God demonstrating “his own love for us,” makes the first reading the more likely here, and most interpreters take it that way.

verse.text: For while we were still weak, at the right time Christ died for the ungodly.
For scarcely will anyone die for a righteous person—though for a good person someone might perhaps even dare to die.
But God demonstrates his own love for us in that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us.
Much more, then, having now been justified by his blood, we will be saved through him from the wrath.
verse.note: The Greek says only “the wrath.” Many translations add “of God” for clarity. The reference is to God’s coming judgment on wrongdoing, which Paul has described earlier in the letter (1:18; 2:5).

verse.text: For if, while we were enemies, we were reconciled to God through the death of his Son, much more, having been reconciled, we will be saved by his life.
And not only that, but we also boast in God through our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom we have now received reconciliation.
Therefore, just as through one man sin entered the world, and through sin death, and so death spread to all people, because all sinned—
verse.note: Paul begins a comparison (“just as…”) and breaks it off at the end of the verse without completing it, turning aside to explain in verses 13–17. The comparison is resumed and completed in verse 18. The dash at the end of verse 12 marks the break.

The Greek connecting phrase is much debated. Most modern scholars and translations take it as “because”; others take it as “with the result that” or “on the basis of which.” The old Latin rendering “in whom all sinned,” meaning in Adam, was influential in Western theology but is not now generally thought to be what the Greek says. Whether “all sinned” refers to each person’s own sins or to humanity’s involvement in Adam’s sin is also disputed.

verse.text: for until the law sin was in the world, but sin is not charged to anyone’s account when there is no law.
Yet death reigned from Adam until Moses, even over those who had not sinned in the likeness of Adam’s transgression. He is a pattern of the one who was to come.
verse.note: The traditional rendering “type” is a technical term of biblical interpretation that few modern readers know. The Greek word means a mold, model or pattern: Adam, as one person whose act affected all, prefigures the Christ who was to come. Some translations have “figure” or “prototype.”

verse.text: But the gracious gift is not like the offense. For if by the offense of the one the many died, much more did the grace of God and the gift that comes in the grace of the one man, Jesus Christ, abound to the many.
verse.note: The word means a wrongful act, a violation of what is right. “Trespass,” the usual rendering, now chiefly suggests entering property without permission; “offense” is used by the King James Version in this chapter and by some modern versions. Paul uses it alongside “sin” and “transgression” (verse 14), which are different Greek words.

verse.text: And the gift is not like what came through the one who sinned. For the judgment followed one offense and led to condemnation, but the gracious gift followed many offenses and led to justification.
verse.note: This Greek word usually means a righteous requirement or a righteous act, and it is rendered “righteous act” in verse 18. Here, set as the opposite of “condemnation,” it must mean a verdict in someone’s favor, and so it is translated “justification,” as in most English versions. A different but related Greek word lies behind “justification” in verse 18.

verse.text: For if by the offense of the one death reigned through that one, much more will those who receive the abundance of grace and of the gift of righteousness reign in life through the one, Jesus Christ.
So then, just as through one offense condemnation came to all people, so also through one righteous act justification that brings life comes to all people.
verse.note: The Greek can also be read “the offense of one man” and, correspondingly, “the righteous act of one man.” Both readings have support among translators. The verse has no verbs in Greek; “came” and “comes” are supplied in English.

verse.text: For just as through the disobedience of the one man the many were made sinners, so also through the obedience of the one the many will be made righteous.
Now the law came in alongside so that the offense might increase; but where sin increased, grace abounded all the more,
so that, just as sin reigned in death, so also grace might reign through righteousness, leading to eternal life through Jesus Christ our Lord.
verse.note: The Greek adjective is formed from the word for “age.” In Jewish usage “eternal life” is the life of the age to come, so the phrase describes a kind of life as well as its unending length. “Eternal” is the standard rendering; a minority of translators render “life of the age to come.”

verse.text: What then shall we say? Should we continue in sin so that grace may increase?
By no means! We who died to sin—how can we still live in it?
Or do you not know that all of us who were baptized into Christ Jesus were baptized into his death?
So we were buried with him through baptism into death, so that, just as Christ was raised from the dead through the glory of the Father, we too might walk in newness of life.
For if we have become united with him in the likeness of his death, we will certainly also be united with him in the likeness of his resurrection.

note.term: united with him in the likeness of his death
note.traditional: planted together in the likeness of his death

verse.note: The Greek says only “we have become joined with the likeness of his death”; “with him” is supplied, as in most modern versions. The alternative is that believers are joined to the likeness itself, perhaps meaning baptism. The second half of the verse is compressed in Greek (“we will also be of the resurrection”), and the words carried over from the first half are filled in here.

verse.text: We know this: our old self was crucified with him so that the body of sin might be rendered powerless, so that we would no longer be slaves to sin,
verse.note: Literally “our old human being.” After the contrast between Adam and Christ in the previous chapter, many interpreters take the phrase to mean the person one was as a member of Adam’s humanity, not merely a part of one’s inner psychology. “Self” is the usual modern rendering and is kept here.

The verb means to put something out of operation or deprive it of force; it is not the ordinary word for destroying. Translations are divided here between “destroyed,” “done away with” and “rendered powerless.” The last is chosen because Paul goes on to speak of the body as still present and still needing to be offered to God (verses 12–13).

verse.text: for the one who has died has been justified from sin.
verse.note: Most versions have “freed” or “set free,” but the verb is Paul’s regular word for “justify,” that is, declare to be in the right or acquit; a different verb is used for “set free” in verses 18 and 22. The thought seems to be that death settles sin’s claim on a person, as a legal case closes when the defendant dies. Greek has a single word-family where English divides between “just/justify” and “righteous/righteousness,” so this verb belongs with “righteousness” later in the chapter.

verse.text: Now if we died with Christ, we believe that we will also live with him,
knowing that Christ, having been raised from the dead, no longer dies; death is no longer his master.
For the death he died, he died to sin once for all; but the life he lives, he lives to God.
So you too must consider yourselves dead to sin but alive to God in Christ Jesus.
Therefore do not let sin reign in your mortal body so that you obey the body’s desires,

and do not present the parts of your body to sin as weapons of unrighteousness, but present yourselves to God as people alive from the dead, and the parts of your body to God as weapons of righteousness.
verse.note: The word can mean tools or implements in general, and most versions have “instruments.” In the usage of the period, and everywhere else in Paul, the plural means weapons or armor, and the surrounding language of reigning and mastery suits a military picture. Many commentators therefore prefer “weapons.”

verse.text: For sin will not be your master, for you are not under law but under grace.
What then? Should we sin because we are not under law but under grace? By no means!
Do you not know that when you present yourselves to someone as slaves for obedience, you are slaves of the one you obey—whether of sin, leading to death, or of obedience, leading to righteousness?
But thanks be to God that, though you were slaves of sin, you obeyed from the heart the pattern of teaching to which you were handed over,

note.term: to which you were handed over
note.traditional: which was delivered to you; to which you were committed

verse.note: One would expect teaching to be handed on to people, but Paul reverses it: the people were handed over to the teaching. The verb is the ordinary one for transferring someone into another’s control, and in this context it pictures slaves passing to a new master. Versions that render “committed” or “entrusted” soften that image.

verse.text: and, having been set free from sin, you were enslaved to righteousness.

I am speaking in human terms because of the weakness of your flesh. For just as you presented the parts of your body as slaves to impurity and to lawlessness, leading to more lawlessness, so now present the parts of your body as slaves to righteousness, leading to holiness.
verse.note: The word can denote the process of being made holy (“sanctification”) or the resulting state of being set apart for God (“holiness”). English versions are divided, and the same word is rendered the same way in verse 22.

verse.text: For when you were slaves of sin, you were free with regard to righteousness.
So what fruit did you have then from the things you are now ashamed of? For the end of those things is death.

note.term: from the things you are now ashamed of

verse.note: The verse can be punctuated differently: “So what fruit did you have then? Things of which you are now ashamed.” Ancient manuscripts had no punctuation, and both readings have scholarly support. The rendering here follows the punctuation of the edition translated, which implies the answer “none.”

verse.text: But now, having been set free from sin and enslaved to God, you have your fruit, leading to holiness, and the end is eternal life.
verse.note: The adjective is formed from the word for “age.” In Jewish usage “eternal life” is the life of the age to come, so the phrase describes a kind of life as well as its unending length.

verse.text: For the wages of sin is death, but the gracious gift of God is eternal life in Christ Jesus our Lord.
verse.note: The word was commonly used for a soldier’s pay or ration money, which fits the military imagery of verse 13. Sin is pictured as a commander or master who pays what is owed, and God as one who gives what is not earned.

The Greek word is formed from the word for “grace” used throughout this chapter, and a Greek reader would hear the connection. “Gracious gift” keeps that link; “gift” or “free gift” is the usual rendering.

verse.text: Or do you not know, brothers and sisters—for I am speaking to people who know the law—that the law rules over a person for as long as that person lives?
verse.note: The Greek plural was the ordinary way to address a mixed group of men and women, and Paul is writing to the whole Roman community. “Brothers” alone now suggests to an English reader that only men are addressed. Many recent translations make the same choice; others keep “brothers” with a footnote.

verse.text: For a married woman is bound by law to her husband while he is living; but if the husband dies, she is released from the law concerning her husband.

So then, while her husband is living, she will be called an adulteress if she comes to belong to another man. But if the husband dies, she is free from the law, so that she is not an adulteress if she comes to belong to another man.

So, my brothers and sisters, you too were put to death to the law through the body of Christ, so that you might come to belong to another—to the one who was raised from the dead—in order that we might bear fruit for God.
For when we were in the flesh, the sinful passions that came through the law were at work in our members, to bear fruit for death.
verse.note: “Flesh” in Paul often means more than the physical body: it names human existence in its weakness and its bent away from God. Here “when we were in the flesh” describes the former condition of people who are still bodily alive, so it cannot mean simply “when we had bodies.” Some translations paraphrase as “sinful nature”; the traditional word is kept here because Paul’s usage shades between senses.

verse.text: But now we have been released from the law, having died to what held us fast, so that we serve as slaves in the newness of the Spirit and not in the oldness of the letter.
verse.note: The verb is the one for a slave’s service, and it picks up the slavery language of the preceding chapter (“enslaved to God”). “Serve” alone loses that connection, which returns in verse 25. Most translations have “serve”; some have “are slaves.”

note.traditional: newness of spirit / the new way of the Spirit

verse.note: Greek manuscripts did not distinguish capital letters, so the word could be God’s Spirit or the human spirit as opposed to the “letter” of a written code. Most modern translators and commentators take it as the Holy Spirit, in view of the similar contrast in Romans 2:29 and 2 Corinthians 3:6 and the argument of chapter 8. Older versions often print lowercase “spirit.”

verse.text: What then shall we say? Is the law sin? By no means! Yet I would not have come to know sin except through the law. For I would not have known coveting if the law had not said, “You shall not covet.”
verse.note: Paul quotes the tenth commandment (Exodus 20:17; Deuteronomy 5:21) without its list of objects. The Greek noun and verb are the general words for desire, here in the bad sense of craving what is not one’s own, and the noun and verb match in Greek as “coveting” and “covet” do here. The scope is wider than envy of a neighbor’s property.

verse.text: But sin, seizing an opportunity through the commandment, produced in me every kind of coveting. For apart from law, sin is dead.
I was once alive apart from law; but when the commandment came, sin sprang to life,

note.term: I was once alive apart from law

verse.note: Who the “I” of verses 7–25 is has been debated since antiquity. It has been read as Paul’s own experience, as Adam facing the commandment in Eden, as Israel receiving the law at Sinai, or as a representative human voice. From verse 14 the verbs shift to the present tense, and interpreters are divided over whether that describes a believer’s continuing struggle or life under the law seen from a Christian standpoint. The translation leaves the question open.

verse.text: and I died; and the commandment that was meant to lead to life was found, in my case, to lead to death.
For sin, seizing an opportunity through the commandment, deceived me and through it killed me.
So the law is holy, and the commandment is holy and righteous and good.

Did what is good, then, become death for me? By no means! Rather, it was sin, producing death in me through what is good, so that it might be shown to be sin—so that through the commandment sin might become sinful beyond measure.
For we know that the law is spiritual; but I am made of flesh, sold under sin.
verse.note: The image is of a person sold as a slave and so placed under a master’s power; sin is pictured as the owner. A first-century reader, living in a slave society, would have heard this at once. Some translations spell it out as “sold into slavery under sin.”

verse.text: For I do not understand what I am carrying out. For I do not practice what I want; instead, what I hate is what I do.

note.traditional: I allow not / I do not understand

verse.note: The verb is the ordinary word for knowing. Most translations take it as “understand”: the speaker is baffled by his own behavior. A minority take it in the sense “acknowledge” or “approve,” which gives “I do not approve of what I do.”

verse.text: But if what I do is what I do not want, I agree with the law that it is good.
But as it is, it is no longer I who carry it out, but the sin that lives in me.
For I know that nothing good lives in me, that is, in my flesh. For the wanting is right at hand for me, but the carrying out of the good is not.
For I do not do the good that I want; instead, the evil that I do not want is what I practice.
But if what I do is what I do not want, it is no longer I who carry it out, but the sin that lives in me.
So I find this law: when I want to do the good, evil is right at hand for me.

note.traditional: a law / this law / this principle

verse.note: Paul plays on the word “law” through verses 21–25. Most interpreters take it here to mean a rule or regular pattern, the “law” that evil is always at hand. Others hold that it still refers to the law of Moses: “I find, as regards the law, that when I want to do the good, evil is at hand.” The word “law” is kept so that the wordplay remains visible.

verse.text: For I delight in the law of God in my inner person,
but I see a different law in my members, waging war against the law of my mind and taking me captive to the law of sin that is in my members.
What a wretched person I am! Who will rescue me from this body of death?

note.traditional: the body of this death / this body of death

verse.note: The Greek word “this” can go with either “body” or “death,” giving “this body of death” or “the body of this death.” Either way the body is one marked out for death, in which sin has been at work. Translations are divided.

verse.text: Thanks be to God through Jesus Christ our Lord! So then, I myself with my mind serve the law of God as a slave, but with my flesh the law of sin.
verse.note: The manuscripts differ here. The reading translated, “Thanks be to God,” is adopted by modern critical editions; many later manuscripts read “I thank God,” which older English versions follow. The sense is little affected.

verse.text: So there is now no condemnation for those who are in Christ Jesus.
For the law of the Spirit of life in Christ Jesus has set you free from the law of sin and death.
verse.note: The Greek text followed here reads a singular “you,” found in several of the earliest manuscripts. Many other manuscripts read “me,” continuing the first-person voice of chapter 7, and a few read “us.” Editors are divided, and the sense of the passage is little affected.

verse.text: For what the law could not do, weak as it was through the flesh, God did. Sending his own Son in the likeness of sinful flesh and as a sin offering, he condemned sin in the flesh,
verse.note: Paul uses “flesh” in this chapter not for the physical body as such but for human nature in its weakness and under the dominion of sin, set against life directed by God’s Spirit. Some modern versions paraphrase it as “sinful nature” or “human nature.” The traditional word is kept because Paul’s contrast of flesh and Spirit depends on it.

The Greek is literally “and concerning sin.” In the Greek Old Testament this exact phrase is the regular term for the sin offering, and many scholars think Paul’s readers would have heard it that way. Others take it more generally as “to deal with sin,” and many English versions have simply “for sin.”

verse.text: so that the righteous requirement of the law might be fulfilled in us, who walk not according to the flesh but according to the Spirit.
For those who are according to the flesh set their minds on the things of the flesh, but those who are according to the Spirit, on the things of the Spirit.
For the mindset of the flesh is death, but the mindset of the Spirit is life and peace,
because the mindset of the flesh is hostility toward God; for it does not submit to God’s law, nor indeed can it.
And those who are in the flesh cannot please God.
But you are not in the flesh but in the Spirit, if indeed the Spirit of God dwells in you. And if anyone does not have the Spirit of Christ, that person does not belong to him.
But if Christ is in you, the body is dead because of sin, but the Spirit is life because of righteousness.
verse.note: The Greek word can mean God’s Spirit or the human spirit, and Greek manuscripts do not distinguish them by capital letters. Many translations take it as the human spirit, “your spirit is alive.” The Greek says “life,” not “alive,” and the next verse speaks of God’s Spirit giving life, which is why the Spirit is preferred here; the question is disputed.

verse.text: And if the Spirit of the one who raised Jesus from the dead dwells in you, the one who raised Christ Jesus from the dead will also give life to your mortal bodies because of his Spirit who dwells in you.

note.term: because of his Spirit who dwells in you
note.traditional: through his Spirit who dwells in you

verse.note: The manuscripts are divided between two grammatical forms that differ by a few letters. The Greek text followed here means “because of his Spirit”; the other reading, adopted by most English versions, means “through his Spirit.” The first makes the indwelling Spirit the reason for the future giving of life, the second the means; the evidence is closely balanced.

verse.text: So then, brothers and sisters, we are debtors—but not to the flesh, to live according to the flesh.
verse.note: The Greek plural was the ordinary way to address a mixed group of men and women as members of one family. “Brothers” alone now suggests to English readers that only men are addressed. Many recent translations render it “brothers and sisters,” while others keep “brothers.” The same rendering is used in verse 29.

verse.text: For if you live according to the flesh, you are going to die; but if by the Spirit you put to death the deeds of the body, you will live.
For all who are led by the Spirit of God are sons of God.
verse.note: Paul uses “sons” here and in verse 19 but “children” in verses 16, 17 and 21, and the translation keeps the two words distinct. “Sons” ties in with the legal language of adoption and inheritance in verses 15 to 17, since in the ancient world an adopted son became an heir. Paul plainly includes women as well as men, and several modern versions translate “children” throughout.

verse.text: For you did not receive a spirit of slavery to fall back into fear, but you received the Spirit of adoption, by whom we cry, “Abba, Father!”
verse.note: The same Greek word stands behind “a spirit of slavery” and “the Spirit of adoption.” The second is taken here as God’s Spirit, who brings about adoption, in line with verses 14 and 16; some translations use lowercase “spirit” for both, meaning a disposition. The word for adoption is a legal term for the formal placing of someone as a son and heir.

verse.text: The Spirit himself bears witness with our spirit that we are children of God.
And if children, then heirs—heirs of God and fellow heirs with Christ, if indeed we suffer with him so that we may also be glorified with him.
For I consider that the sufferings of the present time are not worth comparing with the glory that is going to be revealed to us.
For the creation in eager expectation awaits the revealing of the sons of God.
For the creation was subjected to futility, not willingly but because of the one who subjected it, in hope
that the creation itself will also be set free from slavery to decay into the freedom of the glory of the children of God.
For we know that the whole creation has been groaning together and suffering the pains of childbirth together until now.
And not only that, but we ourselves, who have the firstfruits of the Spirit—we too groan within ourselves as we await adoption, the redemption of our bodies.
For in this hope we were saved. But hope that is seen is not hope; for who hopes for what they see?
But if we hope for what we do not see, we await it with endurance.
In the same way the Spirit also helps us in our weakness. For we do not know what to pray for as we ought, but the Spirit himself intercedes with wordless groans,
and the one who searches hearts knows what the mindset of the Spirit is, because he intercedes for the holy ones as God wills.
verse.note: The traditional “saints” now suggests canonized individuals or people of exceptional virtue. Paul uses the word for all believers as people set apart for God, echoing the language of the Greek Old Testament for Israel. Many translations keep “saints”; others use “God’s people.”

verse.text: And we know that for those who love God all things work together for good, for those who are called according to his purpose.

note.term: all things work together for good
note.traditional: all things work together for good

verse.note: The Greek can be read with “all things” as the subject, as here, or with God as an unexpressed subject: “he works all things together for good.” Some early manuscripts add the word “God” to make the second reading explicit; the Greek text followed here does not. Either way Paul’s point is that God’s purpose stands behind the outcome. The word “his” before “purpose” is supplied for English.

verse.text: For those he foreknew he also predestined to be conformed to the image of his Son, so that he might be the firstborn among many brothers and sisters.
And those he predestined he also called; and those he called he also justified; and those he justified he also glorified.
What then shall we say to these things? If God is for us, who is against us?
He who did not spare his own Son but gave him up for us all—how will he not also, along with him, graciously give us all things?
Who will bring a charge against God’s chosen ones? God is the one who justifies.
Who is the one who will condemn? Christ is the one who died—or rather, who was raised—who is also at the right hand of God, who also intercedes for us.
Who will separate us from the love of Christ? Will affliction or distress or persecution or famine or nakedness or danger or sword?
verse.note: The Greek word was an ordinary term for hardship or oppression pressing on a person. “Tribulation” is now often heard as the name of a specific end-time period, which says more than the Greek does. English versions vary widely here, using “trouble,” “hardship,” “affliction” and “tribulation.”

verse.text: As it is written: “For your sake we are being put to death all day long; we have been considered sheep for slaughter.”
But in all these things we are more than conquerors through the one who loved us.
For I am convinced that neither death nor life, nor angels nor rulers, nor things present nor things to come, nor powers,
verse.note: The word is the ordinary Greek term for a ruler or a ruling office. Standing between “angels” and “powers,” it most likely refers here to spiritual powers thought to hold sway over the world, not to human governments, though Paul does not spell this out. “Principalities” is the older English rendering; several modern versions have “rulers,” and some paraphrase as “demons.”

verse.text: nor height nor depth, nor any other created thing will be able to separate us from the love of God that is in Christ Jesus our Lord.
I am speaking the truth in Christ—I am not lying, and my conscience bears me witness in the Holy Spirit:
I have great sorrow and unceasing anguish in my heart.
For I could wish that I myself were accursed, cut off from Christ, for the sake of my brothers and sisters, my kinsfolk according to the flesh.
verse.note: The Greek word, anathema, is the Septuagint’s term for something handed over to God for destruction and so placed under a curse. The Greek says literally “accursed from Christ”; “cut off” is supplied to make the phrase work in English. The verb “I could wish” is in a past tense that here expresses a wish the speaker knows cannot be granted, and many interpreters hear an echo of Moses’ offer in Exodus 32:32.

verse.text: They are Israelites; theirs are the adoption and the glory and the covenants and the giving of the Law and the worship and the promises;
theirs are the fathers, and from them comes the Christ according to the flesh, who is over all, God blessed forever. Amen.

note.term: who is over all, God blessed forever
note.traditional: who is over all, God blessed for ever

verse.note: The earliest Greek manuscripts have little or no punctuation, and this clause can be read in two ways. Taken with what precedes, as here and in most English versions, it calls Christ “God blessed forever”; with a full stop after “flesh” it becomes a separate doxology, “God who is over all be blessed forever.” The word order favors the first reading, since Paul’s independent doxologies are phrased differently, but a number of scholars and translations prefer the second because Paul rarely if ever calls Christ “God” outright elsewhere.

verse.text: But it is not as though the word of God has failed. For not all who are from Israel are Israel,
nor are they all children because they are Abraham’s offspring; rather, “Through Isaac your offspring will be called.”
That is, it is not the children of the flesh who are children of God, but the children of the promise are counted as offspring.
For the word of promise was this: “About this time I will come, and Sarah will have a son.”
And not only that, but there was also Rebecca, who conceived children by one man, our father Isaac.
For when they had not yet been born or done anything good or bad—so that God’s purpose according to his choice might stand,
verse.note: The traditional word is “election,” which today suggests voting or a technical term of theology. The Greek noun is the ordinary word for a choice or selection, and the phrase describes God’s purpose as one that works by his choosing. The sense is not disputed; most versions keep “election” or write “God’s purpose in election.”

verse.text: not by works but by the one who calls—she was told, “The older will serve the younger,”
just as it is written, “Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated.”
verse.note: The quotation is Malachi 1:2–3, where Jacob and Esau stand for the nations descended from them, Israel and Edom. In biblical idiom “love” and “hate” set side by side can express choosing one over another and not only emotion (compare Genesis 29:30–31; Luke 14:26). Interpreters differ on how far that softens the statement here.

verse.text: What then shall we say? Is there injustice with God? By no means!
For he says to Moses, “I will have mercy on whomever I have mercy, and I will have compassion on whomever I have compassion.”
So then, it depends not on the one who wants or the one who runs, but on God who has mercy.
For the Scripture says to Pharaoh, “For this very purpose I raised you up, so that I might display my power in you, and so that my name might be proclaimed in all the earth.”
So then, he has mercy on whomever he wants, and he hardens whomever he wants.
You will say to me then, “Why then does he still find fault? For who has resisted his will?”
But who indeed are you, a human being, to talk back to God? Will the thing molded say to the one who molded it, “Why did you make me like this?”
Or does the potter not have authority over the clay, to make from the same lump one vessel for honor and another for dishonor?
And what if God, wanting to display his wrath and to make known his power, bore with great patience vessels of wrath made ready for destruction,
verse.note: The Greek participle can give a reason (“because he wanted to display his wrath”) or a concession (“although he wanted to display his wrath, he held back”). The translation leaves this open, as the Greek does. The sentence running through verse 24 is also grammatically incomplete, an “if” with no “then,” which English conveys with “what if.”

The Greek does not say who did the preparing. It can be read as “prepared” by God, as “having made themselves ready,” or simply as a description, “ripe for destruction.” Many point out that for the vessels of mercy in the next verse Paul uses a different, active verb with God as its subject; others hold that God is the implied agent in both.

verse.text: and did so in order to make known the riches of his glory upon vessels of mercy, which he prepared beforehand for glory,
namely us, whom he also called, not only from among Jews but also from among Gentiles?
verse.note: Greek has a single word, ethnos, for a nation and, in the plural, for the non-Jewish peoples, where English uses both “nations” and “Gentiles.” Here and in verse 30 the contrast with Jews and with Israel shows that the second sense is meant.

verse.text: As he also says in Hosea, “I will call those who are not my people ‘my people,’ and her who is not loved ‘loved.’”

text.q: “And in the place where it was said to them, ‘You are not my people,’ there they will be called sons of the living God.”

verse.text: And Isaiah cries out concerning Israel, “Though the number of the sons of Israel be like the sand of the sea, it is the remnant that will be saved;

text.q: for the Lord will carry out his word on the earth, completing it and cutting it short.”

note.term: completing it and cutting it short
note.traditional: he will finish the work, and cut it short in righteousness: because a short work will the Lord make upon the earth

verse.note: The earliest manuscripts have this short form of the quotation from Isaiah 10:22–23. Later manuscripts fill it out from the Greek Old Testament, which is the form the King James Version translates. The meaning of the two participles is itself debated; the likely sense is that the Lord will carry out his sentence completely and without delay.

verse.text: And as Isaiah said beforehand, “If the Lord of Hosts had not left us offspring, we would have become like Sodom and been made like Gomorrah.”
verse.note: Paul, following the Greek version of Isaiah 1:9, leaves the Hebrew word untranslated: “Lord Sabaoth.” It means “of armies,” usually understood as the heavenly forces at God’s command. “Hosts” is the long-established English rendering and is an old word for armies.

verse.text: What then shall we say? That Gentiles, who were not pursuing righteousness, laid hold of righteousness—the righteousness that is by faith;
verse.note: Greek uses one word-family where English has two: “righteous” and “just,” “righteousness” and “justice.” The “injustice” denied of God in verse 14 is the negative of the word translated “righteousness” here. Some scholars prefer “justice” throughout; “righteousness” is kept because “justice” tends to suggest punishment to a modern reader.

verse.text: but Israel, pursuing a law of righteousness, did not reach that law.
Why? Because they pursued it not by faith but as if by works. They stumbled over the stone of stumbling,
as it is written, “See, I am laying in Zion a stone of stumbling and a rock that makes people fall, and the one who believes in him will not be put to shame.”

note.term: a rock that makes people fall

verse.note: The quotation joins two passages of Isaiah: the stone laid in Zion from 28:16, and the stone of stumbling and rock of falling from 8:14. Older versions have “rock of offence,” but the Greek word means something that trips a person up, not something that hurts feelings. “In him” could also be translated “in it,” meaning the stone; Paul applies the stone to Christ, as 10:11 shows.

verse.text: Brothers and sisters, my heart’s desire and my prayer to God for them is for their salvation.
For I testify on their behalf that they have zeal for God, but not in accordance with knowledge.
For, not knowing God’s righteousness and seeking to establish their own, they did not submit to the righteousness of God.
verse.note: Greek has a single word-family where English has two: “righteous” and “just,” “righteousness” and “justice,” and “justify” all translate related forms of one Greek word. “The righteousness of God” here can mean God’s own action to set things right or the right standing that God gives; scholars are divided, and Paul may intend both. “Righteousness” is kept because “the justice of God” would suggest punishment to a modern reader.

verse.text: For Christ is the end of the law, leading to righteousness for everyone who believes.
verse.note: The Greek word can mean a termination, a goal, or an outcome, and each has been defended here. On one reading Christ brings the law’s role to a close; on another he is the goal toward which the law was always heading; many interpreters combine the two. “End” is kept because the English word can carry both senses.

verse.text: For Moses writes that “the person who does the righteousness that comes from the law will live by it.”

note.traditional: Moses writes about the righteousness that is from the law: “The person who does these things will live by them.”

verse.note: Manuscripts differ on the wording of this verse. The text translated here makes “the righteousness that comes from the law” the thing a person does and lives by. Other manuscripts, followed by many translations, have the wording shown as the traditional rendering, which stands closer to Leviticus 18:5, the passage Paul is drawing on.

verse.text: But the righteousness that comes from faith speaks this way: “Do not say in your heart, ‘Who will go up into heaven?’” (that is, to bring Christ down)

note.term: Do not say in your heart

verse.note: In verses 6–8 Paul lets the righteousness that comes from faith speak in the words of Deuteronomy 30:12–14, where Moses says that God’s commandment is not far off in heaven or across the sea but near at hand. The opening words echo Deuteronomy 9:4. Paul adds a comment after each line applying it to Christ, and in verse 7 “the abyss,” the deep or the realm of the dead, stands where Deuteronomy speaks of crossing the sea.

verse.text: or, “Who will go down into the abyss?” (that is, to bring Christ up from the dead).
But what does it say? “The word is near you, in your mouth and in your heart” (that is, the word of faith that we proclaim);
because if you declare with your mouth that Jesus is Lord and believe in your heart that God raised him from the dead, you will be saved.
verse.note: The Greek conjunction can mean “because” or “that.” With “that,” verse 9 states the content of the word of faith; with “because,” it explains why the word is near, in mouth and heart. Translations are divided.

The Greek verb means to state openly or acknowledge publicly. “Confess” is the traditional rendering, but in modern English it mainly suggests admitting guilt, which is not in view here. Some modern translations likewise use “declare.” The words declared could also be rendered “Jesus as Lord.”

verse.text: For with the heart one believes, leading to righteousness, and with the mouth one declares, leading to salvation.
For the Scripture says, “Everyone who believes in him will not be put to shame.”
For there is no distinction between Jew and Greek, for the same Lord is Lord of all, rich toward all who call on him.
For “everyone who calls on the name of the Lord will be saved.”
verse.note: The quotation is Joel 2:32 (3:5 in the Greek version), where “the Lord” stands for the name of Israel’s God. Coming directly after “Jesus is Lord” in verse 9 and “the same Lord is Lord of all” in verse 12, the line is most likely applied by Paul to Jesus, though some interpreters take “Lord” here as God the Father.

verse.text: How then are they to call on one in whom they have not believed? And how are they to believe in one whom they have not heard? And how are they to hear without someone proclaiming?

note.term: one whom they have not heard
note.traditional: him of whom they have not heard

verse.note: Most translations read “of whom they have not heard,” that is, heard about. In Greek, however, this verb with its object in this grammatical case normally means hearing a person speak, not hearing about them, so the sense is probably that Christ himself is heard in the message of those who proclaim him. A number of commentators accept this reading; the traditional one remains possible.

verse.text: And how are they to proclaim unless they are sent? As it is written, “How beautiful are the feet of those who bring good news of good things!”
verse.note: The verb here and the noun in verse 16, traditionally “gospel,” were ordinary Greek words for announcing good news, including public and imperial announcements. “Gospel” now sounds like a religious term or a book title, so “good news” is used; many modern translations do the same in places. The quotation is from Isaiah 52:7, where a messenger announces to Jerusalem that God reigns.

verse.text: But not all have heeded the good news. For Isaiah says, “Lord, who has believed what they heard from us?”
verse.note: The Greek word, quoted from Isaiah 53:1, can mean both the act of hearing and the thing heard, a report or message. Paul uses it twice more in verse 17, and it belongs with “heard” in verses 14 and 18 and with “heeded” in this verse, a compound of the same verb. Rendering it “what is heard” keeps that chain visible; most translations have “our message” or “our report” here and “hearing” in verse 17.

verse.text: So faith comes from what is heard, and what is heard comes through the word of Christ.
verse.note: Many later manuscripts read “the word of God,” which older English versions follow; the earliest witnesses have “the word of Christ.” The phrase can mean the message about Christ or the word Christ himself speaks through his messengers; the Greek does not decide.

verse.text: But I ask, have they not heard? Indeed they have: “Their voice has gone out into all the earth, and their words to the ends of the inhabited world.”
But I ask, did Israel not know? First, Moses says, “I will make you jealous over those who are not a nation; over a nation without understanding I will make you angry.”
verse.note: This is the singular of the word that in the plural is usually translated “Gentiles,” the non-Jewish peoples. Paul reads the line from Deuteronomy 32:21 as pointing to them: God will stir Israel to jealousy through people who had no standing as his nation. The theme returns in chapter 11.

verse.text: And Isaiah is so bold as to say, “I was found among those who were not seeking me; I showed myself to those who were not asking for me.”
But about Israel he says, “All day long I have stretched out my hands to a disobedient and contrary people.”
I ask, then: has God rejected his people? By no means! For I myself am an Israelite, a descendant of Abraham, of the tribe of Benjamin.
God has not rejected his people, whom he foreknew. Or do you not know what the Scripture says in the passage about Elijah, how he appeals to God against Israel?
verse.note: The Greek says simply “in Elijah.” Before chapter and verse numbers existed, a passage of Scripture was located by naming its subject. The reference is to the story in 1 Kings 19, where Elijah complains to God about Israel and receives the reply quoted in verse 4.

text.q: “Lord, they have killed your prophets, they have torn down your altars; I alone am left, and they are seeking my life.”

verse.text: But what does the divine answer say to him? “I have kept for myself seven thousand men who have not bent the knee to Baal.”
In the same way, then, at the present time also there has come to be a remnant, chosen by grace.

note.traditional: according to the election of grace

verse.note: The Greek noun means a choosing or selection. The traditional “election” is accurate as a theological term but now suggests voting, so the word is rendered with “choice” and “chosen” here and in verses 7 and 28. In verse 7 the abstract noun stands for the people chosen.

verse.text: But if it is by grace, it is no longer on the basis of works; otherwise grace would no longer be grace.
What then? What Israel is seeking, it did not obtain. The chosen obtained it, but the rest were hardened,
just as it is written: “God gave them a spirit of stupor, eyes that would not see and ears that would not hear, to this very day.”
And David says: “Let their table become a snare and a trap, a stumbling block and a retribution for them;

text.q: let their eyes be darkened so that they cannot see, and keep their backs bent continually.”

verse.text: I ask, then: did they stumble so as to fall? By no means! Rather, through their misstep salvation has come to the Gentiles, to make Israel jealous.
verse.note: The word ordinarily means a wrongful act, and most versions have “trespass” or “transgression” here. Paul sets it directly beside “stumble” and “fall,” so the picture of a false step is active, and “misstep” keeps that picture while still naming a real failure. Some versions have “stumbling” for the same reason.
