The Greek word means “nations” or “peoples,” and in the plural it is the regular Jewish term for the non-Jewish peoples. English versions render the same word as “Gentiles” or “nations” according to context; throughout this chapter it refers to non-Jews as distinct from Israel.

verse.text: Now if their misstep means riches for the world, and their loss means riches for the Gentiles, how much more will their fullness mean!
verse.note: The word can mean a full number, a completion, or a state of fullness. Many interpreters take it here, and in verse 25 of the Gentiles, as the full number of those who will come in; others take it as Israel’s full restoration in contrast to its present “loss.” The rendering “fullness” leaves both open and keeps the two verses linked.

verse.text: Now I am speaking to you Gentiles. Inasmuch as I am an apostle to the Gentiles, I make much of my service,
verse.note: Most translations have “ministry.” The Greek was an everyday word for service or for a task carried out on someone’s behalf, and it did not denote a religious office. “Service” avoids the modern suggestion of a clerical profession; here it refers to Paul’s commission as apostle to the Gentiles.

verse.text: in the hope that I may somehow make my own flesh and blood jealous and save some of them.
For if their casting aside means the reconciliation of the world, what will their acceptance mean but life from the dead?
verse.note: The phrase most likely means God’s setting Israel aside for a time, balanced by his “acceptance” of them later; this is the majority view. Some scholars read it as Israel’s own rejection of the good news. The word differs from the verb in verses 1–2, where Paul denies that God has rejected his people, so a different English word is used here.

verse.text: If the firstfruits are holy, so is the whole batch of dough; and if the root is holy, so are the branches.
verse.note: Numbers 15:17–21 instructs Israel to offer to God a portion from the first of its dough. Paul’s point is that the dedicated portion makes the whole batch holy. The firstfruits and the root are usually understood as the patriarchs, though some take the firstfruits to be the present remnant of Jewish believers.

verse.text: But if some of the branches were broken off, and you, a wild olive shoot, were grafted in among them and came to share with them in the rich root of the olive tree,

note.term: the rich root of the olive tree
note.traditional: the root and fatness of the olive tree

verse.note: The text translated reads literally “the root of the richness of the olive tree.” Many later manuscripts read “the root and the richness,” which older English versions follow, and a few omit “the root.” The sense is little affected: the grafted branch draws on the nourishing sap of the tree.

verse.text: do not boast over the branches. If you do boast, remember that it is not you who support the root, but the root that supports you.
You will say, then, “Branches were broken off so that I might be grafted in.”
True enough. They were broken off for lack of faith, and you stand by faith. Do not think highly of yourself, but be afraid;
for if God did not spare the natural branches, neither will he spare you.
Consider, then, the kindness and the severity of God: severity toward those who fell, but God’s kindness toward you, provided you continue in his kindness; otherwise you too will be cut off.
And they too, if they do not continue in their lack of faith, will be grafted in, for God is able to graft them in again.

For if you were cut from what is by nature a wild olive tree and, contrary to nature, were grafted into a cultivated olive tree, how much more will these, the natural branches, be grafted into their own olive tree!

For I do not want you to be unaware of this secret, brothers and sisters, so that you will not be wise in your own eyes: a hardening has come upon Israel in part, until the fullness of the Gentiles has come in,
verse.note: Most English versions keep “mystery.” In Jewish Greek of the period the word was the ordinary term for a secret, especially a plan of God that only he can disclose. English “mystery” suggests a puzzle beyond understanding, whereas Paul goes on to state the content plainly.

verse.text: and in this way all Israel will be saved, just as it is written: “The deliverer will come from Zion; he will turn ungodliness away from Jacob.

note.term: and in this way all Israel will be saved
note.traditional: and so all Israel shall be saved

verse.note: The Greek expression normally indicates manner (“in this way”), pointing back to the process just described; some read it as temporal (“and then”). “All Israel” is also disputed: most scholars take it as the Jewish people as a whole, not necessarily every individual, while others take it as the elect of Israel through history or as the whole people of God, Jew and Gentile together.

text.q: And this will be my covenant with them, when I take away their sins.”

verse.text: As regards the good news, they are enemies for your sake; but as regards God’s choice, they are beloved for the sake of their ancestors.
verse.note: The traditional rendering is “gospel,” which is now a religious term or a book title. The Greek was an ordinary word for a public announcement of good news. Many modern translations alternate between the two.

verse.text: For the gifts and the calling of God are irrevocable.
For just as you were once disobedient to God but have now received mercy through their disobedience,
so these too have now been disobedient, so that through the mercy shown to you they too may now receive mercy.

note.term: through the mercy shown to you
note.traditional: that through your mercy they also may obtain mercy

verse.note: In the Greek the words “the mercy shown to you” stand before “so that,” and they can be attached either way. Taken with what follows, as here and in most versions, they give the means by which Israel will receive mercy. Taken with what precedes, the sense is “they have now been disobedient for the sake of the mercy shown to you,” which parallels verse 30 more closely.

verse.text: For God has shut all people up in disobedience so that he may have mercy on all.
Oh, the depth of the riches and the wisdom and the knowledge of God! How unsearchable are his judgments, and how untraceable his ways!
For “who has known the mind of the Lord? Or who has been his counselor?”
Or “who has given to him first, so that he must be repaid?”
For from him and through him and to him are all things. To him be the glory forever. Amen.
So I urge you, brothers and sisters, by the mercies of God, to present your bodies as a living sacrifice, holy and pleasing to God; this is your rational worship.
verse.note: The Greek adjective was a common word, especially among philosophers, for what belongs to reason or befits a rational being. Many modern versions have “spiritual worship,” taking the contrast to be with animal sacrifice, and the King James Version has “reasonable service.” “Rational” keeps the ordinary sense of the word and fits the stress on the renewed mind in the next verse. The noun translated “worship” is the term for service offered to God in a temple.

verse.text: And do not be conformed to this age, but be transformed by the renewing of your mind, so that you may discern what the will of God is—what is good and pleasing and perfect.
verse.note: The Greek word is a time-word meaning an era. Paul shares the Jewish contrast between the present age and the age to come. Many versions keep “world” here, but lexicons give “age” as the sense, and some modern translations use it.

verse.text: For by the grace given to me I say to every one of you: do not think more highly of yourself than you ought to think, but think with sound thinking, each according to the measure of faith that God has apportioned.
For just as in one body we have many members, and the members do not all have the same function,
so we, the many, are one body in Christ, and individually members of one another.
We have gifts that differ according to the grace given to us: if prophecy, in proportion to our faith;

note.traditional: according to the proportion of faith

verse.note: The Greek is literally “according to the proportion of the faith.” Most interpreters take this as the prophet’s own faith, as rendered here. Others take it as “in agreement with the faith,” meaning the content of what is believed. The sentence in verses 6–8 has no main verb in Greek, and many translations supply one such as “let us use them.”

verse.text: if service, in serving; or the one who teaches, in teaching;
verse.note: This was an everyday word for serving or carrying out a task for someone, from waiting at table to delivering a commission. It did not name a religious office. Most translations use “ministry” for church work, which now suggests clergy; standard lexicons list “service” among the glosses.

verse.text: or the one who encourages, in encouraging; the one who shares, with sincerity; the one who leads, with diligence; the one who shows mercy, with cheerfulness.
verse.note: The word’s established sense is singleness or sincerity: giving without mixed motives. Many modern translations render it “generously” or “with generosity,” a sense that fits the context of giving but that lexicographers dispute for this period. The King James Version has “with simplicity.”

note.traditional: he that ruleth; the one who leads

verse.note: The verb can mean to preside or lead, and also to care for or give aid, as a patron would. Because it stands between sharing and showing mercy, some scholars prefer “the one who gives aid.” Most translations take it as leadership, as here.

verse.text: Let love be without pretense. Abhor what is evil; cling to what is good.
In brotherly love be devoted to one another; in honor lead the way for one another.
In diligence do not be slack; in spirit be fervent; serve the Lord.
verse.note: The verb literally means to boil. The Greek can refer to the human spirit, as rendered here, or to the Holy Spirit: “be aglow with the Spirit.” Translators and commentators are divided.

verse.text: In hope rejoice; in affliction endure; in prayer persevere.
Share in the needs of the holy ones; pursue hospitality.
verse.note: The word is used of all believers as people set apart for God, echoing the Septuagint’s language for Israel. “Saints” now suggests canonized individuals or people of exceptional virtue. Many translations keep “saints”; others use “God’s people.”

verse.text: Bless those who persecute—bless, and do not curse.
verse.note: Many manuscripts add “you,” and most translations include it. The Greek text followed here omits it. The verb is the same one translated “pursue” in verse 13, so Paul moves from pursuing hospitality to blessing those who pursue with hostile intent.

verse.text: Rejoice with those who rejoice; weep with those who weep.
Think of one another in the same way; do not think lofty thoughts, but keep company with the lowly. Do not be wise in your own eyes.

note.traditional: men of low estate; the lowly

verse.note: The Greek form can be masculine, meaning lowly people, or neuter, meaning humble tasks or circumstances. The second reading would give “give yourselves to humble things,” in contrast to the “lofty thoughts” just mentioned. Most translations take it of people.

verse.text: Repay no one evil for evil; take thought for what is honorable in the sight of all people.
If possible, as far as it depends on you, live at peace with all people.
Do not avenge yourselves, beloved, but leave room for the wrath, for it is written: “Vengeance is mine; I will repay, says the Lord.”
verse.note: The Greek says only “the wrath,” but the quotation that follows, from Deuteronomy 32:35, shows that God’s judgment is meant. Many translations add “of God” for clarity. The words “says the Lord” are not part of the Deuteronomy text; Paul adds them to mark God as the speaker.

verse.text: Rather, “if your enemy is hungry, feed him; if he is thirsty, give him something to drink; for in doing this you will heap burning coals on his head.”
verse.note: The verse quotes Proverbs 25:21–22 in its Greek form. The meaning of the image is disputed. Most interpreters think it pictures the burning shame an enemy feels when repaid with kindness, which may lead to a change of heart. Others take it as a picture of the divine judgment the enemy will face if unmoved.

verse.text: Do not be conquered by evil, but conquer evil with good.
verse.note: The Greek verb is the ordinary word for winning a battle or contest and is related to the noun for “victory.” Most translations have “overcome” here, which in modern English can suggest merely getting past a difficulty. The meaning is not in dispute; “conquer” keeps the note of victory.

verse.text: Let every person be subject to the governing authorities, for there is no authority except from God, and those that exist have been set in place by God.
verse.note: The Greek is literally “every soul,” a Septuagint idiom in which the word simply designates an individual. Nothing is implied about an inner or immaterial part of a person. Most modern translations likewise have “every person” or “everyone.”

The phrase is literally “authorities that are over [one].” The great majority of scholars take it as the civil officials a resident of Rome would deal with, as the references to the sword and to taxes in verses 4–7 suggest. A minority view has held that angelic powers standing behind the state are also in view, since Paul elsewhere uses the same noun for spiritual powers.

verse.text: So whoever opposes the authority has resisted what God has set in place, and those who have resisted will bring judgment on themselves.

note.term: what God has set in place

verse.note: Verses 1–2 play on a single Greek word family: “be subject,” “set in place,” “opposes,” and this noun all share one root having to do with ordering or arranging. The noun means an arrangement or directive. It is rendered here to echo “set in place” in verse 1 so that some of the repetition survives in English.

The judgment could be the penalty imposed by the authorities themselves, or God’s judgment, or God’s judgment carried out through the authorities. The following verses, which speak of the ruler’s sword as an instrument of wrath, favor the last, but the Greek does not specify. The older rendering “damnation” says more than the word does.

verse.text: For rulers are no cause of fear to good conduct, but to evil. Do you want to be unafraid of the authority? Do what is good, and you will have praise from it,

for it is God’s servant for your good. But if you do what is evil, be afraid, for it does not carry the sword for nothing. It is God’s servant, an avenger who brings wrath on the one who practices evil.
verse.note: The words “avenger” and “wrath” pick up 12:19, where readers were told not to avenge themselves but to leave room for the wrath, since vengeance belongs to God. Paul presents the ruler’s punishment of wrongdoing as one way that wrath is carried out. The chapter division obscures this connection.

verse.text: Therefore it is necessary to be subject, not only because of the wrath but also because of conscience.
For this is also why you pay taxes, for the authorities are God’s public servants, devoting themselves to this very thing.
verse.note: This is a different word from “servant” in verse 4. In ordinary Greek it named someone who performed a public service or held a public office, and in the Septuagint it is also used of those serving in the temple. “Ministers” now suggests clergy or, in some countries, cabinet members. Whether Paul intends a sacred overtone here is debated.

verse.text: Pay everyone what you owe them: tax to the one owed tax, toll to the one owed toll, fear to the one owed fear, honor to the one owed honor.

note.term: tax to the one owed tax, toll to the one owed toll
note.traditional: tribute to whom tribute is due; custom to whom custom

verse.note: Two kinds of payment are named. The first was the direct tax or tribute levied on subject peoples, and the second covered indirect charges such as customs duties and tolls on goods. Many modern translations have “taxes” and “revenue.”

note.term: fear to the one owed fear
note.traditional: respect to whom respect is owed

verse.note: The noun is the same one translated “fear” in verse 3, and it is kept here so the link is visible. Many modern translations soften it to “respect.” Some interpreters think Paul distinguishes fear, owed to God, from honor, owed to rulers, as in 1 Peter 2:17. Most take both as owed to human authorities of different rank.

verse.text: Owe no one anything, except to love one another, for the one who loves the other person has fulfilled the law.

note.term: the one who loves the other person has fulfilled the law
note.traditional: he that loveth another hath fulfilled the law

verse.note: The Greek could also be construed as “the one who loves has fulfilled the other law,” meaning the law of Moses as distinct from civil obligations. Nearly all translators and commentators take “the other” as the object of “loves,” as here, which fits the quotation about the neighbor in verse 9.

verse.text: For the commandments “You shall not commit adultery,” “You shall not murder,” “You shall not steal,” “You shall not covet,” and any other commandment there may be, are summed up in this saying: “You shall love your neighbor as yourself.”
Love does no evil to a neighbor; therefore love is the fulfillment of the law.
And do this knowing the time: it is already the hour for you to wake from sleep, for our salvation is nearer now than when we came to believe.
verse.note: Manuscripts are divided between “you” and “us,” which differ by one letter in Greek. The edition translated here reads “you.” Many early and later witnesses read “us,” which matches “our salvation” in the next clause.

verse.text: The night is far gone, and the day has drawn near. So let us throw off the works of darkness and put on the armor of light.
verse.note: The edition translated here reads a verb meaning “throw off,” found in some early witnesses. Most manuscripts and most critical editions have a milder verb meaning “put off” or “lay aside,” which is Paul’s usual word for removing clothing in this kind of image. The sense is little affected.

verse.text: Let us walk decently, as in the day: not in carousing and drunkenness, not in promiscuity and debauchery, not in strife and jealousy.
verse.note: The Greek word is literally “beds,” in the plural, a common euphemism for sexual intercourse; here it means illicit sexual encounters. “Sexual immorality” is avoided because it is the usual English for a different and broader Greek term.

verse.text: Instead, put on the Lord Jesus Christ, and make no provision for the flesh, to satisfy its desires.
Welcome the one who is weak in faith, but not to pass judgment on his opinions.

note.term: but not to pass judgment on his opinions
note.traditional: but not to quarrel over opinions

verse.note: The Greek phrase is compressed and can be read two ways. The noun usually means evaluating or distinguishing, which gives “passing judgment on opinions” and fits the chapter’s repeated warnings against judging. It can also mean a dispute, and most modern translations take it that way: “not for quarrels over opinions.”

verse.text: One person believes he may eat anything, while the weak person eats only vegetables.
The one who eats must not look down on the one who does not eat, and the one who does not eat must not judge the one who eats, for God has welcomed him.
Who are you to judge someone else’s household servant? Before his own master he stands or falls. And he will stand, for the Lord is able to make him stand.
verse.note: “Master” here and “the Lord” in the next sentence are the same Greek word. Paul moves from the picture of a household servant answerable only to his own master to the believer’s Lord, and the wordplay continues through verse 9.

verse.text: One person judges one day to be above another; another judges every day to be alike. Let each be fully convinced in his own mind.

The one who observes the day observes it for the Lord. And the one who eats, eats for the Lord, since he gives thanks to God; and the one who does not eat, it is for the Lord that he does not eat, and he gives thanks to God.
For none of us lives for himself, and none of us dies for himself.
If we live, we live for the Lord, and if we die, we die for the Lord. So whether we live or die, we belong to the Lord.
For this is why Christ died and came to life: so that he might be Lord of both the dead and the living.
But you—why do you judge your brother? Or you—why do you look down on your brother? For we will all stand before the judgment seat of God,
verse.note: The earliest manuscripts read “of God”; many later ones, followed by the King James Version, read “of Christ,” probably under the influence of 2 Corinthians 5:10. The word for “judgment seat” is the raised platform from which a magistrate heard cases.

verse.text: for it is written: “As I live, says the Lord, every knee will bow to me, and every tongue will give praise to God.”
verse.note: Paul quotes Isaiah 45:23 in its Greek form, with an opening formula found in Isaiah 49:18. In the Greek Scriptures this verb with “to God” regularly means to acknowledge God openly with praise or thanks, as often in the Psalms. “Confess to God” now suggests admitting sins, which is not the point; some translations have “acknowledge God.”

verse.text: So each of us will give an account of himself.

note.traditional: give account of himself to God

verse.note: Many manuscripts, and most English translations, add “to God” at the end of the sentence. Some important early witnesses lack the words, and the Greek text followed here omits them. The meaning is not affected, since verse 10 has already named God’s judgment seat.

verse.text: So let us no longer judge one another. Make this your judgment instead: not to put a stumbling block or a trap in your brother’s way.

note.traditional: hindrance, obstacle, or occasion to fall

verse.note: Paul pairs two near-synonyms for something that brings a person down. The second word is rendered “stumbling block” elsewhere in this translation, but here that wording is taken by the first word, so “trap” is used—a sense the word has in the Greek Scriptures. Most translations have “hindrance” or “obstacle,” which are milder than the Greek.

verse.text: I know and am persuaded in the Lord Jesus that nothing is unclean in itself; but to the one who considers something unclean, to that person it is unclean.
verse.note: The Greek word ordinarily means “common” or “shared.” Among Greek-speaking Jews it had come to mean ritually defiled, the opposite of holy or clean, and was used especially of food forbidden by the Law or tainted by contact with what was forbidden. Paul’s point concerns ritual status, not hygiene.

verse.text: For if your brother is distressed because of food, you are no longer walking in love. Do not by your food destroy the one for whom Christ died.
So do not let the good that is yours be slandered.
verse.note: Paul does not say what “your good” is. Most interpreters take it as the freedom of the strong to eat anything, which would be brought into disrepute if it harmed others. Others take it as the gospel or the blessings the whole community shares. The verb is the one traditionally transliterated “blaspheme,” which in Greek covered defamatory speech of any kind.

verse.text: For the kingdom of God is not eating and drinking, but righteousness and peace and joy in the Holy Spirit;
verse.note: Greek has a single word-family where English has two (righteous and just, righteousness and justice). Here most interpreters take the word to mean right conduct toward others in the community. Some take it as the right standing with God that Paul has described earlier in the letter.

verse.text: for the one who serves Christ in this way is pleasing to God and approved by people.
So then, let us pursue what makes for peace and for building one another up.
Do not tear down the work of God for the sake of food. Everything is indeed clean, but it is wrong for the person whose eating is a stumbling block.

note.term: whose eating is a stumbling block

verse.note: The Greek is literally “the person who eats through a stumbling block.” This translation takes it of the strong believer whose eating trips up someone else, which suits the commands on either side. It can also be read of the weak believer who eats against his own conscience and so stumbles himself, as in verse 23.

verse.text: It is good not to eat meat or drink wine or do anything by which your brother stumbles or is made to fall or is weak.

note.term: or is made to fall or is weak
note.traditional: or is offended, or is made weak

verse.note: Several early manuscripts end the sentence at “stumbles,” and most modern translations follow them. The Greek text translated here includes the longer reading, which is also early and widely attested. “Is made to fall” renders a verb the King James Version translates “is offended”; it refers to being brought down in one’s faith, not to hurt feelings.

verse.text: The faith that you have, keep to yourself before God. Blessed is the one who does not judge himself in what he approves.
But the one who has doubts is condemned if he eats, because it is not from faith; and everything that is not from faith is sin.
verse.note: In this context “faith” is the settled confidence before God that a particular action is permitted, as in verses 2 and 22. Most interpreters therefore take the closing sentence as a statement about acting against one’s own conviction. It has also long been read as a general principle that whatever does not spring from Christian faith is sin.

verse.text: We who are strong ought to bear the weaknesses of those who are not strong, and not to please ourselves.
Each of us should please our neighbor for what is good, to build them up.
For even Christ did not please himself, but as it is written: “The insults of those who insult you have fallen on me.”
For whatever was written beforehand was written for our instruction, so that through endurance and through the encouragement of the Scriptures we might have hope.
Now may the God of endurance and encouragement grant you to be of the same mind with one another, in accordance with Christ Jesus,
so that together, with one voice, you may glorify the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ.
Therefore welcome one another, just as Christ also welcomed you, to the glory of God.
For I say that Christ has become a servant of the circumcised for the sake of God’s truth, to confirm the promises made to the fathers,
and so that the Gentiles might glorify God for his mercy. As it is written: “Therefore I will give thanks to you among the Gentiles, and sing praise to your name.”

note.term: and so that the Gentiles might glorify God for his mercy

verse.note: The Greek of verses 8–9 is compressed and its grammar is disputed. The rendering takes the Gentiles’ glorifying God as a second purpose of Christ’s becoming a servant of the circumcised, which is the majority view. Others read it as a second statement dependent on “I say”: that the Gentiles, for their part, glorify God for mercy.

The Greek word is the ordinary word for “nations” or “peoples”; in the plural, in Jewish usage, it means the non-Jewish peoples. It is the same word in each of the quotations in verses 9–12, where English versions of the Old Testament often have “nations.” Paul strings these passages together because each contains it.

verse.text: And again it says: “Rejoice, you Gentiles, with his people.”
And again: “Praise the Lord, all you Gentiles, and let all the peoples extol him.”
And again Isaiah says: “The root of Jesse will come, the one who rises to rule the Gentiles; in him the Gentiles will hope.”
verse.note: Paul quotes Isaiah 11:10 from the Greek version, which differs from the Hebrew, where the root of Jesse “stands as a signal for the peoples.” The verb for “rises” is also a common word for rising from the dead, and many interpreters think Paul heard that overtone here, though the quotation does not require it.

verse.text: Now may the God of hope fill you with all joy and peace in believing, so that you may overflow with hope by the power of the Holy Spirit.
I myself am convinced about you, my brothers and sisters, that you yourselves are full of goodness, filled with all knowledge, and able also to admonish one another.
But on some points I have written to you rather boldly, by way of reminding you, because of the grace given to me by God
to be a minister of Christ Jesus to the Gentiles, serving the good news of God as a priest, so that the offering of the Gentiles may be acceptable, made holy by the Holy Spirit.
verse.note: The Greek was an ordinary word for an announcement of good news, used also of public and imperial proclamations. “Gospel” is the traditional rendering, but it now sounds like a religious term or the name of a book. Many modern translations alternate between the two.

Paul describes his mission in the language of temple worship: the words behind “minister,” “serving as a priest,” and “offering” were all used of sacrificial service. Most interpreters take the offering to be the Gentiles themselves, presented to God through Paul’s work. The Greek could also mean an offering that the Gentiles bring.

The Greek verb is built directly on the word for “holy,” the same word used in “Holy Spirit” in this phrase, and “made holy” keeps that link audible. “Sanctified” is the traditional rendering and means the same thing; the choice is one of clarity, not of meaning.

verse.text: So I have my boast in Christ Jesus in what concerns God.
For I will not dare to speak of anything except what Christ has accomplished through me to bring the Gentiles to obedience, by word and deed,
by the power of signs and wonders, by the power of the Spirit—so that from Jerusalem and all the way around to Illyricum I have fully proclaimed the good news of Christ,
verse.note: The manuscripts divide three ways here: “the Spirit,” “the Spirit of God,” and “the Holy Spirit.” The Greek text followed prints the shortest reading, on the view that the longer forms are scribal expansions. Many translations follow “the Spirit of God.” The sense is not affected.

verse.text: and so making it my ambition to proclaim the good news not where Christ has already been named, so that I would not build on someone else’s foundation,
but as it is written: “Those who were not told about him will see, and those who have not heard will understand.”
This is also why I have so often been hindered from coming to you.
But now I no longer have room to work in these regions, and for many years I have longed to come to you
whenever I travel to Spain. For I hope to see you as I pass through and to be sent on my way there by you, once I have first enjoyed your company for a while.

note.traditional: whensoever I take my journey into Spain, I will come to you

verse.note: In the Greek, Paul’s sentence in verses 23–24 breaks off and never reaches its main verb; the translation completes it as smoothly as English allows. Later manuscripts mend the break by adding “I will come to you” after “Spain,” which is why those words appear in the King James Version.

This verb regularly meant more than saying goodbye: it was used of equipping travelers with provisions, money, or companions for the next stage of a journey. Paul is signaling that he hopes the believers in Rome will support his mission to Spain.

verse.text: But now I am going to Jerusalem in service to the holy ones.
verse.note: The word is used of all believers as people set apart for God, echoing the Greek Old Testament’s language for Israel. “Saints,” the traditional rendering, now suggests canonized individuals or people of exceptional virtue. Other translations use “God’s people” or “the Lord’s people.”

verse.text: For Macedonia and Achaia were pleased to share something with the poor among the holy ones in Jerusalem.
verse.note: The noun is the one usually translated “fellowship”; here it names a concrete act of sharing, the money Paul collected from his largely Gentile churches for poor believers in Jerusalem. Most translations say “make a contribution.” “Share” is used so that the link with the related verb in verse 27, “have shared in,” stays visible.

verse.text: They were pleased to do so, and indeed they are in debt to them. For if the Gentiles have shared in their spiritual things, they ought also to minister to them in material things.
So when I have completed this and have set the seal on this fruit for them, I will set out for Spain by way of you.

note.term: set the seal on this fruit

verse.note: The exact image is uncertain. Goods were sealed to guarantee that they arrived intact, so the phrase most likely means delivering the collection safely and formally into the hands of the Jerusalem believers, and many translations simply say “delivered.” “Fruit” is the collection, perhaps seen as the produce of the mission among the Gentiles.

verse.text: And I know that when I come to you, I will come in the fullness of Christ’s blessing.
I urge you, brothers and sisters, through our Lord Jesus Christ and through the love of the Spirit, to struggle alongside me in your prayers to God on my behalf,
that I may be rescued from the disobedient in Judea and that my service for Jerusalem may be acceptable to the holy ones,
verse.note: The verb’s ordinary meaning is to disobey or refuse to comply, and it stands in contrast to the “obedience” of the Gentiles in verse 18. Many translations have “unbelievers,” since the disobedience in view is refusal of the good news; others have “the disobedient.” Paul means those in Judea who reject the message about Jesus.

verse.text: so that by God’s will I may come to you with joy and find rest in your company.
May the God of peace be with you all. Amen.
I commend to you our sister Phoebe, who is also a deacon of the assembly in Cenchreae,
verse.note: The Greek word ordinarily means someone who serves or carries out a task for another, and this translation usually renders it “servant.” Here it is tied to a particular assembly (“of the assembly in Cenchreae”), which suggests a recognized role, so “deacon” is used. Whether Paul means a defined office or simply that Phoebe served that community is disputed, and many translations have “servant.”

The traditional rendering is “church,” which is near-universal and which readers readily understand. A first-century hearer knew the word as a civic gathering and as the Septuagint's term for Israel assembled, whereas “church” now suggests a building or an institution. This translation uses “assembly” throughout so that the reader can see it is one Greek word.

verse.text: so that you may welcome her in the Lord in a manner worthy of the holy ones, and stand by her in whatever matter she may need you, for she herself has been a patron of many, and of me as well.
verse.note: The traditional rendering is “saints,” which many translations keep; others use “God's people.” The word is applied to all believers as people set apart for God, echoing the Septuagint's language for Israel. “Saints” now suggests canonized individuals or people of exceptional virtue.

Older translations have “helper” or “succorer”; several recent ones have “patron” or “benefactor.” In the period the word and its masculine counterpart were used of a person of means and standing who protected and supported others, so more than general helpfulness is implied. The Greek also plays on a related verb: the Romans are to “stand by” Phoebe because she has stood up for many.

verse.text: Greet Prisca and Aquila, my coworkers in Christ Jesus,
who risked their own necks for my life; not only I but also all the assemblies of the Gentiles give thanks to them.
verse.note: The Greek word means “peoples” or “nations,” and in the plural it commonly refers to the non-Jewish peoples. This translation renders it “Gentiles” in that sense and “nations” where peoples as such are meant; it is one Greek word throughout.

verse.text: Greet also the assembly in their house. Greet my beloved Epaenetus, who is the firstfruits of Asia for Christ.
Greet Mary, who has labored much for you.
Greet Andronicus and Junia, my kinsfolk and fellow prisoners, who are outstanding among the apostles and who were in Christ before I was.
verse.note: The Greek form could in theory be a woman's name, Junia, or a man's name, Junias, depending on accentuation, which the earliest manuscripts do not mark. Junia was a common Latin woman's name, while Junias as a male name is not securely attested, and early interpreters took the person to be a woman. Most scholars and recent translations now read Junia; she and Andronicus may have been husband and wife.

The phrase can mean that Andronicus and Junia were distinguished members of the group called apostles, or that they were well known to the apostles. Most interpreters, ancient and modern, favor the first reading, which is followed here. A minority argue for the second. If the first is right, “apostles” is used in the wider sense of commissioned emissaries, not the Twelve.

The word means relatives, and Paul uses it in Romans 9:3 for his fellow Jews as a people. Most interpreters think he means fellow Jews here and in verses 11 and 21 rather than members of his own family, but closer kinship cannot be ruled out. “Kinsfolk” and “kinsman” leave both possibilities open.

verse.text: Greet Ampliatus, my beloved in the Lord.
Greet Urbanus, our coworker in Christ, and my beloved Stachys.
Greet Apelles, tested and approved in Christ. Greet those who belong to the household of Aristobulus.
Greet Herodion, my kinsman. Greet those of the household of Narcissus who are in the Lord.
Greet Tryphaena and Tryphosa, who labor in the Lord. Greet the beloved Persis, who has labored much in the Lord.
Greet Rufus, chosen in the Lord, and his mother, who is mine too.
Greet Asyncritus, Phlegon, Hermes, Patrobas, Hermas, and the brothers and sisters with them.
Greet Philologus and Julia, Nereus and his sister, and Olympas, and all the holy ones with them.
Greet one another with a holy kiss. All the assemblies of Christ greet you.
Now I urge you, brothers and sisters, to watch out for those who create divisions and stumbling blocks contrary to the teaching you learned, and turn away from them.
For such people are slaves not to our Lord Christ but to their own belly, and by smooth talk and flattery they deceive the hearts of the unsuspecting.
verse.note: Most translations have “serve.” The verb is the one related to the ordinary Greek word for a slave, and denotes belonging to and working for a master. The stronger rendering keeps it distinct from the different word-group translated “servant” in this translation.

verse.text: For your obedience has become known to everyone. So I rejoice over you, but I want you to be wise about what is good and innocent about what is evil.
The God of peace will soon crush Satan under your feet. The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with you.
Timothy, my coworker, greets you, and so do Lucius, Jason, and Sosipater, my kinsfolk.
I, Tertius, who wrote down this letter, greet you in the Lord.
verse.note: Letters were commonly dictated to a secretary, and Tertius, who penned this one for Paul, adds his own greeting here. “In the Lord” may go with “greet you,” as rendered, or with “wrote down”; the Greek word order allows either.

verse.text: Gaius, who is host to me and to the whole assembly, greets you. Erastus, the city treasurer, greets you, and so does our brother Quartus.
verse.note: The Greek title means a manager or steward, here of the city, most likely Corinth, from which the letter appears to have been sent. It indicates a post in the city's financial administration, but exactly which office, and of what rank, is uncertain. Such a post could be held by a person of high status or by a public slave or freedman.

verse.text: The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with all of you. Amen.

note.term: The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ be with all of you. Amen.

verse.note: This verse is absent from several of the earliest manuscripts, and many modern translations omit it or place it in a footnote; it largely repeats the blessing in verse 20. The Greek edition translated here includes it. The same edition does not print the closing doxology that most English Bibles number as verses 25–27, because that passage appears at different places in the manuscripts and is absent from some.
